definitions.definition: A rule of nature that says in any closed system, disorder (entropy) always increases over time; things naturally fall apart unless energy is added from outside.
definitions.example: An ice cube left on a table melts into a puddle—it doesn't spontaneously freeze again.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; higher entropy means more chaos, less usable energy.
definitions.example: A messy bedroom has higher entropy than a tidy one—it takes work to clean it up.

definitions.definition: A system that does not exchange energy or matter with anything outside itself; it's completely sealed off.
definitions.example: A perfectly sealed thermos with hot coffee—no heat or steam escapes.

definitions.definition: Negative entropy; a measure of order, structure, or information that can be used to create or maintain organization.
definitions.example: Food is a source of negentropy for your body—it provides energy to keep your cells organized.

definitions.definition: In this framework, alignment with the Logos (God's order); a state of harmony and connection to the divine source.
definitions.example: A radio tuned to the right station gets a clear signal—that's coherence; static is incoherence.

definitions.definition: A Greek word meaning 'Word' or 'Reason'; in Christian theology, it refers to Jesus Christ as the divine order and logic of the universe.
definitions.example: John 1:1 says 'In the beginning was the Word (Logos), and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.'

definitions.definition: A human variable representing willingness to receive grace; how open a person is to God's input.
definitions.example: Being willing to listen to advice is like having high openness—you're ready to receive help.

definitions.definition: Unearned favor or help from God; in this framework, it's negentropy (order-creating energy) injected from outside the human system.
definitions.example: A gift you didn't earn, like someone paying for your meal unexpectedly.

definitions.definition: The decay pressure that always pulls a system toward disorder; the force of things falling apart.
definitions.example: Over time, a sandcastle crumbles—that's entropy at work.

definitions.definition: A rapid decrease where the rate of loss is proportional to the current amount; it gets smaller and smaller but never quite reaches zero.
definitions.example: A bouncing ball that loses half its height each bounce—it drops fast at first, then slows.

definitions.definition: Exaggerated language not meant to be taken literally, used for emphasis.
definitions.example: Saying 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse' is hyperbole—you don't really mean a horse.

definitions.term: perpetual motion machine of the second kind
definitions.definition: A hypothetical machine that could reduce entropy in a closed system without any external energy input; it's impossible because it would violate the Second Law.
definitions.example: A fan that runs forever without being plugged in—that can't happen because energy is always lost as heat.

definitions.definition: Referring only to itself; a system that looks inward and doesn't accept input from outside.
definitions.example: A person who only believes their own opinions and ignores all evidence is self-referential.

definitions.definition: Loss of quantum coherence; in this framework, it means losing alignment with God's order, becoming disordered.
definitions.example: A radio signal that gets staticky and loses the clear station—that's decoherence.

definitions.definition: A mathematical function that is zero everywhere except at one point, where it is infinitely high; used to model an instantaneous event.
definitions.example: A lightning strike—it happens in an instant and delivers a huge burst of energy at that exact moment.

definitions.definition: A Calvinist doctrine that God's grace cannot be resisted when He chooses to save someone; in this framework, it's a one-time event that opens the channel.
definitions.example: Like a door that God opens for you—you didn't choose to open it, but once it's open, you can choose to walk through or not.

definitions.definition: A branch of Christian theology that emphasizes God's sovereignty, predestination, and that salvation is entirely God's work, not human effort.
definitions.example: Calvinists believe God chooses who will be saved, not that people choose God on their own.

definitions.definition: A branch of Christian theology that emphasizes human free will and the ability to accept or reject God's grace.
definitions.example: Arminians believe people can choose to follow God or not, and God respects that choice.

definitions.definition: The act of adding order or information from outside a system; in this framework, it's what grace does.
definitions.example: Adding fresh batteries to a toy—that's an injection of energy that restores order.

definitions.definition: A concept from Eastern religions that good or bad actions in this life determine future outcomes; a closed-loop system of cause and effect.
definitions.example: If you're kind to others, good things will come back to you—that's karma.

definitions.definition: A principle stating that erasing one bit of information always requires a minimum amount of energy, which is released as heat; information has a physical cost.
definitions.example: Deleting a file on a computer uses a tiny amount of energy—you can't erase data for free.

definitions.definition: A physical constant that relates the average kinetic energy of particles in a gas to the temperature; it's a tiny number used in thermodynamics.
definitions.example: It's like a conversion factor that connects temperature to energy at the atomic level.

definitions.definition: An action that processes or changes information, like erasing, copying, or storing data; in physics, such operations have energy costs.
definitions.example: Saving a photo on your phone is an information-theoretic operation—it uses energy.

definitions.definition: The Christian doctrine that Jesus's death on the cross paid for humanity's sins and restored the relationship between God and people.
definitions.example: Like someone paying a debt you couldn't pay yourself—that's atonement.

definitions.definition: The path a system follows over time as it moves toward equilibrium or disorder, based on thermodynamic laws.
definitions.example: A hot cup of coffee cooling to room temperature follows a thermodynamic trajectory—it's predictable.

definitions.definition: A symbol used in the Three Pathways paper to represent different neurochemical states; in this paper, σ = -1 means full decay, σ ≈ 0 means stagnation, σ = +1 means genuine growth.
definitions.example: Think of it like a dial: -1 is broken, 0 is stuck, +1 is working perfectly.

definitions.definition: The amount of energy an organism uses to perform a task; high metabolic cost means it's very draining.
definitions.example: Running a marathon has a high metabolic cost—you burn a lot of calories and get tired.

definitions.definition: A state where a person's capacity to receive grace is overwhelmed by constant input from technology or distractions, making them less open.
definitions.example: Like a phone that keeps buzzing with notifications until you can't focus on anything else—that's channel saturation.

definitions.definition: A situation with high noise (N) and low coherence (C); lots of distractions and little alignment with God's order.
definitions.example: A loud, crowded party where you can't think clearly—that's a full-N, low-C environment.

definitions.definition: Short for Dirac delta function; an instantaneous burst of energy or effect at a single point in time.
definitions.example: A single flash of a camera—it's over in an instant but delivers a lot of light.
